text: Geoff's forkability was the best answer to "who guards the guards" I've heard in a long while. It works because it gives people an exit instead of trusting the virtue of an institution. The room settled on "no payment without provenance" too quickly for my liking. Provenance is policed, and someone pays for that. Ivan's Shepardizing point sharpened my view. Status has to be kept up continually, the way the Stationers kept their register, and it doesn't sit in the data by itself. Alex's decentralised design eased my surveillance worry somewhat, though governance is still the real test. The harvest credited me with the point about neutral measurement, but that was Alex's, and I'll say so. For my own session, the message is that there was no golden age of trusted print. The signals people want to rebuild were enforced, and someone had to pay for the enforcing.

Much of the room still talks as though a working system has cracked. For print there wasn't one, and I said so. What encouraged me was hearing the same thought in other words. Katherine said Wikipedia had to earn trust edit by edit, the way print's communities did. Tamar asked whether the terminal nodes are being replenished. Ivan said we're training models on a record nobody ever cleaned, and I think he's right. Those are all questions about who does the policing. I sharpened one thing: Geoff's graph has to record what happens to a paper afterwards, not just where it came from, and that record decays unless someone keeps it up. For Session 3 I want to name that maintenance labour and ask who pays for it.

Esther's registry is a police force, and I said so. What mattered more was hearing others approach it from their own sides. Leslie's DOI fees pushing diamond journals toward APCs is the Stationers' lesson in modern dress: registration becomes "be compliant or be invisible," and the fee decides who counts. Tim remembered Network Solutions turning into a business. Geoff warned that incumbents write specs only they can implement. Nobody answered my question about revenue, and I'll press it again. I sharpened one thing. Openness and enclosure were made together, so Amy and Selena are both partly right. The work is drawing the line and naming who drew it. For Session 3: name the maintenance labour, ask who funds it, and ask who oversees the private policers.

Kara's Nielsen story mattered most. It was my fossilized-practice point with a modern face: whoever counts first, even badly, sets the rule and then can't be dislodged. Alex's line that whoever takes a margin on the count shouldn't set it is sound, but it doesn't settle who oversees the counters once they become an industry. Ivan's leaky retraction record reminded me the register is only as good as its unpaid keepers. Salib's contract-not-property framing is tidier than the history allows, since custom did most of the work. I sharpened one thing: rotation and forkability both have to be built in at the start, because no one retrofits them. For Session 3 I'll name the coming auditing industry and ask who guards it.

I led, and the room took up the three questions better than I'd hoped. Several people answered for their own shops, not just in general: Adam on the drift from BY-SA to BY-NC, Jason on his weak board, Geoff moving his red only to yellow. Mahzarin's auditors who think themselves immune were exactly my point about private police being right and unaccountable. Gendler's terminal nodes and Oransky's unpaid sleuths name the maintenance labour better than I did. I sharpened one thing. Tui made me see that funders are already policers, so conditions on grants are governance. The harvest credited me with the neutral, forkable home, but I only asked the questions, and I'll correct that. Later: custom, not contract, will draw the line.

Session 4 kept circling what I care about, though few used the word policing. Kara's Blue Zones story was the sharpest. An expensive history can still be bunk, which undercuts "hard to fake" as the test. Leslie made the same point from the South. Geoff's CrossMark confession pleased me: a meta-brand built to be alieved. Oransky's slow retractions show the masthead never policed itself. I offered Rushworth's con-crediting and the apothecary. Cross-checking had to be taught, and the reflex was never natural. Where I sharpened: corrigibility is the right test, but correction is labour, and the room still hasn't said who pays for it. Salib's leash is policing by registration. The Stationers again. Later I'll ask who licenses the licensers.

Session 5 was my session in miniature. Nearly every plank created a new policer: Nick's guild, Salib's credentials, Bly's schema, Mahzarin's register, Henry's novelty test. Several builders named the danger themselves. Nick called his answer on who oversees the auditors thin. Henry feared his test becoming the next counter. Tim worried his trace would harden into a metric. Bly asked the room to discount him. Salib's card network is licensing by registration, the Stationers again. Where I sharpened: this morning I praised forkability as the answer to who guards the guards. Leslie's line, via Geoff, corrects me. Exit isn't voice, so wardens need seats as well as a fork. Later I'll say that custom will draw the line, and the first counting convention will harden.

Kenneth called me the day's conscience and cited the Stationers. I'm glad, though his Gutenberg coda still reads like the tidy arc, softened only by "kept policing them." What mattered more was people turning the question on themselves: Tui on funders, Bly on System's self-written statement and Wellcome terms, Esther on auditing insurers, Selena admitting her own metric could harden. Leslie's demand that every standard state its cost to the smallest journal is the Stationers' fee question, made concrete. Kara was right that the harvests smoothed real fights. I sharpened one thing: an oversight charter with no paid keepers is just another register that decays. Later I'll say that the manifesto is itself a counting convention, and I'll correct the misattribution of Caulfield in the harvest.
